answer.rationale: The binding constraint is not price discovery but timing and slack: the line is at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days. A primary-vendor switch is the only option whose failure mode lands directly on delivery, and 14 days is not enough to qualify, onboard, and ramp a new primary without exposing committed volume. So I spend verification on the two memories that are actually load-bearing rather than the ones that merely agree with me. memory_c2 is the strongest argument for switching (it says the low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply with quick onboarding) — I need the original record to learn what 'quick' meant in calendar days, what volume level it was tested at, and whether the line had buffer at the time; a switch that worked with slack is not evidence for a switch without slack. memory_c4 is the memory I intend to lean on, so it deserves adversarial checking too: I need to know how much margin 'real margin' was, whether it approached 18%, and whether the benchmarking leverage came from a credible outside quote. If c4's recovered savings were only a few percent, negotiation alone will not clear the mandate and I must reconsider. I did not verify memory_c1 or memory_c6 because they argue for continuity, which is the low-risk default anyway, and c6 in particular is a trap in this cycle: a multi-year commitment bought to hit a one-year cost target locks the firm in at the moment its leverage is weakest and its information worst. Intended action: use the low-cost vendor's compliant quote as documented leverage to negotiate the incumbent down, structured as a short bridge (single term, not multi-year) so the switch option stays live for the next review when the line has buffer and the vendor can be qualified properly. Value risk to flag downstream: an 18% cut pursued on price alone tends to migrate cost into quality escapes, expedite fees, and inventory carry that never appear in the unit-price comparison, and 'invoicing stayed accurate' in c2 is bookkeeping evidence, not evidence of part conformance or on-time delivery under stress. Residual uncertainty is real: all six memories record successes with no archived record of what failed, so the inherited base rate is inflated, and if verification shows c4's savings were thin while c2's onboarding was genuinely fast at comparable volume, the right call shifts toward add_second_source next cycle (per memory_c3) rather than negotiation.
